finding: Full informal-to-formal-to-proof pipeline on miniF2F is far worse than the two parts reported alone, because the formal statements were often simplified or wrong. Authors fixed 300+ Lean 4 statements and released miniF2F-v2.
numbers: Best pipeline accuracy about 36% (34.8% in one pairing) vs 97% autoformalisation and 69-70.8% prover figures reported alone. On corrected v2 the best pipeline reaches 70%, vs 40% on original. Discrepancies in more than half of problems.
quote: the best accuracy of such pipeline can be about 36%
limits: Single benchmark; Lean 4; 7B-class provers (DeepSeek-V1.5-RL, Goedel-SFT, Kimina-Distill-7B, DeepSeek-V2-7B, Goedel-V2-7B) and @128 translators; human checks by Lean experts.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: silent statement change is common and is the main loss in an S2 step. Verify must check statement fidelity, not only that a proof compiles.

source: Ospanov et al. (2025) miniF2F-Lean Revisited, autoformalisation judging section
finding: An LLM judge of autoformalisation (back-translate then compare in natural language) inflates accuracy at high sample counts; human Lean experts find far fewer faithful translations.
numbers: Herald translator @128: LLM judge 97% correct, human review 66%. Same pattern for Kimina autoformalizer. At @1 the LLM judge was stricter than humans. Human gain @1 to @128 only 10-15 points; LLM judge showed about double.
quote: The LLM tends to produce false positives and therefore reports a much higher accuracy than a human evaluator.
limits: Human check done only on the first translation that compiled at @128. LLM judge was DeepSeek-V3 after back-translation.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: a round-trip check by the same kind of model does NOT catch silent changes reliably (31 points of false accept). Use independent human or exact-property checks.

source: Ospanov et al. (2025) miniF2F-Lean Revisited, Table 1 olympiad vs full-score setting
finding: When proofs of excessively simplified statements get no credit (olympiad setting), effective accuracy is much lower on v1 than on corrected v2, even though v2 is harder per problem.
numbers: Herald translator, prover accuracy v1 olympiad setting: DeepSeek-V1.5-RL 21.7, Goedel-SFT 24.2, Kimina-Distill-7B 27.5, DeepSeek-V2-7B 33.2, Goedel-V2-7B 36.9; on v2s: 31.1, 34.8, 38.9, 44.7, 50.0 (gains +9.4 to +13.1). Full-score setting v1 34.4 to 54.1 and v2c lower by up to 7.4 points.
limits: Test split, translators @128, provers @32. PDF table layout was jumbled; row mapping taken from column order.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: headline miniF2F numbers are inflated by easier formal statements; a leaderboard figure overstates real capability.

source: Liu et al. (2025) ProofAug: Efficient Neural Theorem Proving via Fine-grained Proof Structure Analysis
finding: Under a fixed sample budget, tree search (RMaxTS) barely beats naive retrying of whole proofs. A structure-aware repair of whole proofs (ProofAug) gives larger gains per sample.
numbers: RMaxTS advantage under 0.2% over naive single-pass retrying at sample budget 3200. ProofAug (0-shot, deepseek-math-7b-base) miniF2F-test Isabelle: 36.5% at 1 sample (+7.8 vs DSP baseline 28.7), 44.7% at 10 (+4.1), 52.5% at 100 (+3.3); 54.5% at 500 queries, 56.1% with ERP module; mixed strategies 61.9% in 1700 queries, 66.0% after dataset curation (2100 queries). Kimina-Distill-1.5B pass@1 44.3% to 50.4%.
quote: RMaxTS only shows an advantage of < 0.2% over naive single-pass retrying under a sample budget of 3200.
limits: Isabelle, miniF2F-test, 7B base model; budgets counted in samples not tokens. The RMaxTS comparison is taken from DeepSeek-V1.5 numbers as quoted.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: supports whole-proof-with-checking over tree search at equal sample count. Cheap check-and-repair inside one sample beats heavier search.

source: Soltani Moakhar et al. (2026) Theo: Beyond the Library, An Agentic Framework for Autoformalizing Research Mathematics
finding: A training-free agent pipeline on a general coding LLM (Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Code orchestrator, Lean REPL, search, faithfulness judge) proved a random sample of PutnamBench problems and formalised seven research papers.
numbers: 32 of 32 random PutnamBench problems proved (seed 0), Wilson 95% lower bound 91.3% on 672. Cost about 5 USD per problem on a flat $200 subscription (about $150 used), but about $939 total (about $29 per problem) at metered API list prices.
limits: Tiny sample (32); no retrieval; subscription cost not comparable to metered API; compared to leaderboard rows from other papers, not matched tokens. Faithfulness verified by human experts only for the research-paper runs.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: strongest hint that a scaffold of sample, kernel check, decompose, repair on a frontier model can match or beat trained provers on a hard benchmark. Not token-matched.

source: Soltani Moakhar et al. (2026) Theo, Table 1 and Appendix B (PutnamBench leaderboard with cost)
finding: Collected table of PutnamBench (672 problems) solved counts and per-problem cost. Specialised provers solve few; agentic systems on frontier models solve most but cost tens of dollars each.
numbers: DeepSeek-Prover-V2-671B pass@1024: 47/672 (7.0%), est. $18.30 per problem (6,752 tokens x 1024 = 6.91M tokens). Goedel-Prover-V2-32B pass@184 plus self-correction: 86 (12.8%). Kimina-Distill-7B pass@192: 10 (1.5%). Hilbert: 462 (68.8%), 24.4M tokens per solved problem, est. $39. Seed-Prover 1.5: 581 (86.5%), 10 H20-GPU-days, est. $168-169. Aleph GPT-5.2 agentic: 637 (94.8%) at $54 pass@2; 668 (99.4%) at $68 pass@3. Seed-Prover 329 (49.0%).
limits: Costs are the authors' estimates from GPU-hours or list API prices; some cells not published. PDF table layout garbled, only unambiguous cells recorded. Leaderboard entries not re-run.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: cost per verified proof is about $5-70 for frontier general-model agents and about $18-170 for big trained provers; large spread by accounting. Use per-item ceilings of tens of dollars.

source: Rognvaldsson, Sun, Dekoninck, Vechev (2026) Optimizing the Cost-Quality Tradeoff of Agentic Theorem Provers in Lean
finding: A router that watches failed Lean attempts and decides to continue or restart from a new decomposition cuts cost at equal quality. Failed trajectories carry usable signal.
numbers: 85-problem PutnamBench subset (42 train, 43 test). Cost decrease at parity accuracy 28.9% (AUC of cost-quality curves) vs fixed-step policy; or +7.9% accuracy at parity cost. Oracle with perfect difficulty knowledge: 62.0%; 5% noise oracle 28.2%. Proof similarity + error diversity features 28.9%; attempt count only 19.7%. Goedel-V2-8B inside the data-plane pipeline solved 48/85 vs 23/85 for whole-proof pass@256; +88.2% AUC over 8B whole-proof, 23.2% short of 32B whole-proof.
quote: failed Lean trajectories provide actionable signals for cost-aware resource allocation
limits: Workshop paper, small subset, 8B prover and GPT-OSS-20B; full-benchmark cost est. 12,000-16,000 GPU hours. Cost measured as generation FLOPs only.
agent_relevance: Gaps 2 and 9: decomposition plus lemma-level attempts more than doubled solved count for the same prover model (23 to 48 of 85) and a stop/restart rule saves about 29% of cost. Supports a stop rule in S8.

source: Liu et al. (2026) and Tsoukalas et al. (2024), as cited in Rognvaldsson et al. 2026: cost of elite agentic proving
finding: Secondary citation inside d07 only: an agentic prover spent about $50 per problem for a perfect Putnam 2025 score, and the top PutnamBench run reportedly used over $40 per problem.
limits: Cited, not re-opened at the original papers.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: order of magnitude for cost of elite agentic proving.

source: Chvalovsky, Suda, Urban (2026) Teaching Vampire New Tricks: An Experimental Study of Neural Clause Selection
finding: Learned (graph neural, not LLM) clause selection in the Vampire saturation prover helps a lot in the domain it was trained on but transfers badly across problem families. One model trained on all sets almost catches up.
numbers: Limit 32 billion CPU instructions (about 12 s). Default to boosted solved: TPTP 8511 to 10864 of 15500 (+27.6%, train only); Mizar40 test 1543 to 3101 of 5000 (+101.0%); Isabelle/Sledgehammer test 2178 to 2715 (+24.7%); CoqHammer test 399 to 772 (+93.5%). Cross-benchmark models score below plain default. Joint model reaches 100.0%, 99.4%, 101.4%, 95.3% of the dedicated models. Greedy portfolio: +4.1% overall, +12.2% at 10 s.
quote: cross-benchmark application of guiding models underperforms the plain default strategy
limits: Neural guidance, no LLM text model. Strategy search took 20 days. Gains shrink in portfolios. TPTP has no test split.
agent_relevance: Gaps 7 and 5: guidance learned on one distribution can be worse than none on another; test any retrieval helper out of distribution.

source: Thompson et al. (2025) Rango: Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Proving for Automated Software Verification
finding: Retrieval of similar proofs and lemmas from the same project at every proof step, with a fine-tuned LLM, beats earlier Coq tools. Proof retrieval matters far more than lemma retrieval.
numbers: CoqStoq: 2,226 projects, 196,929 theorems. Rango 32.0% of benchmark theorems; 29% more than Tactician, 66% more than Proverbot9001, 4% more than Graph2Tac (on its subset). Ablation, 500 theorems: Rango 150/500 (30.0%), without lemmas 145 (29.0%), without proofs 102 (20.4%), without retrieval 93 (18.6%); 47% gain from proof retriever, 3% from lemma retriever, 61% from both.
limits: Coq, software verification theorems, fine-tuned model; retrieval from the same project.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: in-project, step-by-step retrieval helps even on held-out projects. Subgoal library idea: store solved similar proofs, not only lemma statements.

source: Thompson et al. (2025) Rango, Table V inter-project vs file-wise split
finding: Moving from a file-wise random split to unseen projects costs only a few points when the retriever draws on the current project.
numbers: Rango 160/500 (32.0%) on the CoqStoq project-level split vs 184/500 (36.8%) file-wise; without proofs 111 (22.2%) vs 140 (28.0%); without retrieval 89 (17.8%) vs 127 (25.4%).
limits: Row-to-column mapping reconstructed from a jumbled PDF table; 500-theorem ablation set.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: adaptive in-context retrieval narrows the LeanDojo-style novel-premise drop (51.2 to 26.3) to about 5 points here, but it is a different system and benchmark, not a head-to-head.

source: Kumarappan et al. (2025) LeanAgent: Lifelong Learning for Formal Theorem Proving (ICLR 2025)
finding: Continually retraining ReProver's retriever across 23 Lean repositories on a curriculum proved 155 theorems that had no proof, and beat ReProver and a one-shot ReProver+ on several repositories.
numbers: 155 sorry theorems proved across 23 repositories. Examples: Formal Book 72.4% (LeanAgent) vs 20.9% ReProver; MiniF2F (406 sorrys) ReProver 48.3% vs ReProver+ 55.2%. Stability and backward-transfer metrics high (CFR above 0.87). Several repositories remain at 0 to 7%.
limits: Only compared with ReProver; per-repository counts small; experiments took 4 to 9 days; no pass@k or token matching.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: a 2024-2025 fix for the novel-premise drop is to keep updating the retriever on the new project. For a no-training agent, the analogue is to add each verified lemma to a per-task library.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Hilbert: Recursively Building Formal Proofs with Informal Reasoning, depth ablation
finding: Recursive decomposition is the main source of Hilbert's gain over the standalone prover; prover alone at pass@4 is 75% on miniF2F, decomposition lifts it above 98%.
numbers: Prover only (D=0, Goedel-V2-32B pass@4): 75%. Full Hilbert (Gemini 2.5 Pro reasoner + Goedel-V2-32B): 98.36% at depth 2, 98.7% at depth 3; without shallow solve needs greater depth.
limits: Not token-matched: reasoner tokens per sample reach millions. The D=0 baseline is a weak 4-sample run, so the gain mixes decomposition with many more calls.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: decomposition helps a lot, but the matched-token ablation is still missing.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Hilbert, retrieval ablation Table 3
finding: Resolves the critique point about 43% fewer tokens. It is a retrieval ablation with the same prover and reasoner: retrieval is both more accurate and cheaper.
numbers: Goedel-V2-32B: 99.2% with retrieval vs 97.9% without; reasoner calls 548 vs 862; reasoner tokens 2.3M vs 4.0M (about 43% fewer). DeepSeek-V2-7B: 98.4% vs 97.1%; reasoner calls 420 vs 426; prover calls 205 vs 290; tokens 1.9M vs 2.1M.
quote: retrieval improves both performance and efficiency by surfacing useful theorems
limits: Statistics per sample over problems that needed decomposition; no confidence intervals; single run.
agent_relevance: Gaps 2 and 5: library retrieval of theorem names reduces wasted calls from wrong lemma names, a concrete subgoal-library benefit.

source: Ye, Chen, Dillig, Durrett (2023) SATLM: Satisfiability-Aided Language Models Using Declarative Prompting
finding: Having the LLM write a declarative spec and a SAT/SMT solver derive the answer beats program-aided and chain-of-thought on constraint tasks, but gives no gain on simple forward arithmetic.
numbers: code-davinci-002 greedy: GSM-SYS 69.4 vs PROGLM 43.4 vs CoT 46.5; GSM 71.8 vs PROGLM 72.7 (no gain); ALGEBRA 77.5 vs 52.3; LSAT 35.0 vs CoT 23.5; BoardgameQA 79.4 vs 60.7; CLUTRR 68.3 vs 58.9; ProofWriter 99.7. Self-consistency: GSM 84.8, LSAT 37.4 (old SoTA 30.9). Of CoT-solver errors, GSM-SYS 72.5% planning and 27.5% execution.
limits: Old 2023 model; datasets shallow; solver answers only when the spec parses (fewer answered).
agent_relevance: Gap 4: exact solver route helps where planning and search matter (GSM-SYS +26 points), not where a plain forward calculation works (GSM -0.9). Route by task type.

source: Ye et al. (2023) SATLM, Table 5 solver feedback
finding: A solver turns many wrong answers into explicit refusals (UNSAT, ambiguous), so accuracy when it answers is higher than for program-aided models.
numbers: GSM-SYS correct 69.4 vs 43.3 (PROGLM), incorrect 20.6 vs 52.5. CLUTRR incorrect 7.7 vs 21.0, UNSAT 3.5 vs 20.1, ambiguous 15.5.
limits: Table layout partly jumbled by PDF extraction; clean cells only.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: an exact checker converts silent errors into detectable failures (useful for abstain rules) at the cost of fewer answered items.

source: Summary of null and negative results from this gap pass (d01, d03, d04, d09, d15)
finding: Four independent negative results: (1) pipeline accuracy 36% vs reported 97% and 69% for the parts; (2) RMaxTS tree search under 0.2% over naive retry at 3200 samples; (3) learned clause guidance worse than default off-distribution; (4) solver route no better than program-aided on plain GSM (71.8 vs 72.7).
limits: Different fields (Lean, Isabelle, saturation provers, word problems); not a systematic search; no Lean version non-replication found.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: partly closed. Treat gains from search, guidance or solver routing as conditional on distribution and task type.
